html:
This is the capstone of the roadmap. Where phases 1-15 taught you one skill at a time, this file hands you three full engagements at the academy's case company, BrightLogistics, and asks you to run them end-to-end as a Business Analyst. Each use case is a complete journey: discovery, documentation, design, and change — from a blank page to artifacts a build team and a developer could implement in the repo's Salesforce org. Do the work in this file first, and only open Phase 17: Use Case Solutions afterwards to compare. Your portfolio gets stronger from the redo, not from the first read.

Learning Objectives

  • Run a greenfield CRM rollout discovery from zero — no system, no data model, no digitized process...
  • Pair a stakeholder register with a RACI matrix across sponsor, operations, drivers, and billing...
  • Capture manual, email-and-Excel "as-is" processes as swimlanes and redesign them as to-be targets...
  • Write and approve a traceable 12-15 requirement BRD in the repo's Business_Requirement__c object...
  • Produce a user-story map and a two-sprint prioritized backlog...
  • Perform a legacy-migration gap analysis with a fit-gap matrix scored by severity times frequency...
  • Design data-cleaning and quarantine requirements for migrated legacy data...
  • Plan UAT for migrated billing scenarios and gate it on signed exit criteria...
  • Turn post-launch adoption failure into an audit, a retraining plan, and a 60-day owned recovery plan...
  • Build sponsor dashboards that compare baseline to target and drive one decision each...
  • Represent at least one journey end-to-end in Salesforce with evidence in force-app/...

How to Use This File

Each use case is written like an engagement brief you would receive on day one. You own the outcome; there is no hidden requirement set to "discover." Work the way the roadmap taught you:

  1. Attempt before you verify. Every milestone has acceptance criteria below, but no worked answers. Your first draft is the learning experience. Open 17-Use-Case-Solutions.md only after you have a deliverable to compare.
  2. Hand your work to a developer. Every deliverable names the "artifact you hand to a build team" — tables, documents, and repo objects such as Stakeholder__c, Business_Requirement__c, User_Story__c, UAT_Test_Case__c, and Process_Map__c. If a developer would have to make a business decision that you did not, the milestone is not done.
  3. Store evidence in the repo. The org artifact lives under force-app/main/default/ (objects, fields, flows, classes, reports, dashboards, permission sets). Store your plans, matrices, and decision logs alongside the metadata in the developer Business Analyst Roadmap/ folder. Test classes in force-app/main/default/classes/ are your proof that the model works.
  4. Reuse the objects the academy built for you. Six custom objects, six flows, eleven service classes, seven triggers, one platform event, one approval process, one permission set (Business_Analyst), one dashboard and two reports exist for you to learn by building. You design the business data; the academic tooling records your analysis.
  5. Score yourself against the KPI. BrightLogistics buys outcomes: lead-to-dispatch under 4 hours, 80% or more auto-assignment, zero silent loss of legacy billing behavior, and adoption that moves. Every requirement you write must trace back to one of those outcomes.

Use Case 1 — New CRM Rollout Discovery (BrightLogistics)

Business Context

BrightLogistics is a 40-person logistics and freight brokerage. The founder and CEO, Greg Nweshi, is the executive sponsor. Sales and operations run on a workbook-and-inbox culture: a basic web form captures inbound leads, those leads are emailed to a shared inbox, and a dispatcher reads them 1-2 days later, re-types the details into Excel, and manually calls a carrier to dispatch the freight. There is no CRM, no shared pipeline view, and no way for leadership to see lead sources, conversion, or response times.

Enter the project: "BrightLogistics CRM rollout" — a Salesforce org (orgName Business Analyst RoadMap Lab, apiVersion 68.0) that captures, qualifies, routes, and dispatches leads faster.

The deal is measured on two KPIs approved by Greg:

KPICurrentTargetDeadline
Lead-to-dispatch cycle time~48 hoursUnder 4 hoursGo-live + 60 days
Inbound leads auto-assigned without human re-entry0%80% or moreGo-live + 60 days

Your constraint from phase 1: the solution must be configurable where possible — objects, fields, flows, assignment rules, approval processes — escalating to Apex only when the platform cannot express the behavior.

Business Requirements

As an engagement brief, you are given outcomes to deliver, not a solution. Your discovery must confirm and refine these twelve outcomes into testable requirements by the end of the phase (the final BRD must hold 12-15 requirements):

  1. Every inbound web-form submission becomes a Salesforce record automatically, with no email-inbox step.
  2. Duplicate leads are flagged or suppressed before a dispatcher wastes work on them.
  3. Every lead is assigned to an owner or queue automatically, without human re-entry.
  4. No qualifying lead may age past 4 hours without an alert or escalation.
  5. Dispatch records the carrier, rate, and ETA as structured data, not prose.
  6. Unassigned or queued work is visible to managers so handoff gaps surface.
  7. Truckers/drivers can acknowledge assigned loads without calling the office.
  8. The sales team can see each lead's full history and source.
  9. Data quality is guarded at entry (required fields, value ranges, no free-text email-only leads).
  10. Access is role-appropriate: reps own their records, managers see the queue, Greg sees the numbers.
  11. Reports prove lead-to-dispatch cycle time and auto-assignment rate factually.
  12. A sponsor dashboard compares baseline to target and drills into detail.

Your "as-is" captures the current 48-hour pain explicitly — the email inbox, the Excel re-key, the manual carrier call — because those pain points are what justify the to-be targets.

Data Model You Must Design

You start at zero and must propose the core objects. Design the business model and the analytic tooling the academy built for you:

  • Business data (your proposal): a web-lead object (standard Lead or a custom record), a customer/shipper master (Account), a dispatch/disposition object that records carrier, rate, and ETA, plus the fields that make the KPIs computable — timestamps for lead received and dispatched, an auto-assignment flag, and a source field.
  • Analytic tooling (existing in the repo, build as you go): Stakeholder__c (with Influence__c, Interest__c, Power_Score__c, Interest_Score__c, RACI__c, Engagement_Level__c) for M1; Process_Map__c (with Step_Count__c, Actor_Count__c, Cycle_Time_Days__c, As_Is_Description__c, To_Be_Description__c) for M2; Business_Requirement__c (with Requirement_Type__c, Priority__c, Status__c, Value_Score__c, Acceptance_Criteria__c) for M3; User_Story__c (with Story_Points__c, Priority__c, Priority_Score__c) for M4; UAT_Test_Case__c for traceability.

For each object you must specify: fields, types, picklist values, required/defaults, and Lookup vs Master-Detail decisions — and be ready to defend why a Lead is not crammed into an Account field.

What You Will Apply

  • Phases 2-3: stakeholder register with power/interest scores and RACI; three discovery workshops that produce as-is and to-be swimlanes with metrics.
  • Phases 4-5: a 7-section BRD, 12-15 numbered testable requirements, and a data dictionary for the core objects.
  • Phases 6-7: a story map, INVEST stories, and a two-sprint prioritized backlog using the academy's weighted scoring (BacklogPrioritizationService, flow Backlog_Prioritization_Scoring).
  • Phases 9-10: automation choices (routing, alerts, approvals) and report/dashboard requirements that make the KPIs verifiable.
  • Repository evidence: your plans live beside metadata in force-app/main/default/; passing test classes prove the model.

Milestones with Acceptance Criteria

Each milestone below is a buyable document — a build team or developer could take it and implement without making a business decision.

M1 — Stakeholder Register and RACI

#Acceptance criterion
1Register lists at least 6 stakeholders by role (sponsor, operations, drivers, billing, admin, dispatcher)
2Every row has power (1-5) and interest (1-5) scores plus a stated engagement strategy
3All four power/interest quadrants are represented with at least one stakeholder each
4RACI matrix covers at least 4 real activities of this rollout with exactly one Accountable per activity
5Register is modeled as Stakeholder__c data the RSVP flow (Stakeholder_RSVP_Tracking) could track
6Engagement plan explains how Greg's High-power/High-interest role differs from the Dispatcher SME's

M2 — Three Discovery Workshops and As-Is/To-Be Swimlanes

#Acceptance criterion
1Three workshop agendas exist, each timeboxed (agenda times sum to the session length, 60-90 minutes)
2Each agenda names a decision to be made that day and the RACI owner of that decision
3At least two as-is swimlanes (lead intake, dispatch/handoff) each with a trigger, an end point, and marked pain points
4At least two to-be swimlanes show every step reduced or eliminated, and each remaining step earns its place
5As-is vs to-be metrics table records steps, actors, cycle time, and handoff count before and after
6Maps are captured as Process_Map__c records with Cycle_Time_Days__c proving 48h (as-is) against <4h (to-be)

M3 — BRD and Traceable Requirement List

#Acceptance criterion
1BRD follows the 7-section structure: background, scope (in/out explicit), stakeholders, process summary, FR, NFR/Data/Reporting, assumptions/open questions
212-15 numbered requirements (R-101...) each in one sentence, each Must/Should/Could prioritized
3Every requirement is testable — each has a pass/fail acceptance criterion a tester could run
4Every requirement is traceable to a stakeholder source and to the KPI it serves
5Traceability is end-to-end: every requirement links to at least one story (M4) and one UAT test case
6Requirements are created as Business_Requirement__c records and the sign-off uses the repo's approval process and Requirement_Approval_Routing flow

M4 — User-Story Map and Prioritized Backlog for Two Sprints

#Acceptance criterion
1Story map shows a backbone (capture, qualify, route, dispatch, follow up, report) with stories under each
2At least 12 stories, each INVEST-compliant with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria
3Backlog is scored with a defined value/effort model and ranked (evidence of Priority_Score__c)
4Two sprints are committed with a stated team capacity; sprint 1 delivers the KPI-critical slicing (auto-capture, dedupe, routing)
5Nothing in sprint 1 depends on an unordered backlog item (stories are Independent)
6Each sprint is small enough for a developer to complete and demo (no story above roughly a 3-5 point estimate)

M5 — Data Dictionary for the Core Objects

#Acceptance criterion
1Dictionary covers every proposed business object (web lead, customer, dispatch) plus the analytic objects you used
2Every field has: name, type, picklist values, required/default, and business meaning
3Relationship decisions (Lookup vs Master-Detail) are justified per pairing
4No open design decisions remain — a build team can implement field-by-field without asking you
5Dictionary aligns with the repo naming convention (__c custom fields, standard objects for standard business nouns)

Success Checklist

  • KPI 1: requirement exists proving lead-to-dispatch under 4 hours, and a report/dashboard makes it measurable
  • KPI 2: requirement exists proving 80%+ auto-assignment, measured at day 60
  • A senior BA could open your folder and start the conversation with "what did you decide?"
  • A developer could implement from your data dictionary without inventing business rules
  • Your artifacts exist in both prose form and as repo evidence (metadata + passing tests)

Use Case 2 — Legacy System Migration Gap Analysis (BrightLogistics billing/files)

Business Context

BrightLogistics' CRM (Use Case 1) is live. Now the company wants to retire its legacy billing and file-handling stack: a 20-year-old on-prem desktop billing system ("FreightBill") plus a network-drive folder of rate PDFs, invoices, and scanned proof-of-delivery documents. The legacy software is unsupported, locked to one office machine, and gives the auditors nothing but spreadsheets.

The mandate is one platform: Salesforce carries billing, invoices, payment status, refunds, holds, and document files — losing none of the billing behavior, even the messy rules the office invented over two decades. Every legacy rule must become a documented requirement or an explicit, agreed de-scope. Nothing may be silently dropped at cutover.

ConcernReality todayTarget
Billing systemOn-prem desktop DB, single machineSalesforce Order/invoice model with payment status
RefundsManual form + manager signatureApproval chain in-platform
Holds/disputesSticky notes and a shared spreadsheetStructured holds with owners and aging
Customer filesNetwork-drive PDFs, loosely namedSalesforce Files attached to records
Data qualityDuplicate customers, empty phone, stale addressesClean master, quarantined suspects, list of what stayed behind

Business Requirements

  1. Every legacy capability and rule is inventoried — nothing is assumed to carry over or to be dropped without a record.
  2. Fit-gap states, for each legacy capability, whether Salesforce is a fit, partial fit, gap, or no fit, scored by severity (1-5) times frequency (1-5).
  3. Every "no fit" produces a documented decision with options (configure, extend, package, build) and a decision owner — not an automatic custom build.
  4. Migration lands data with a target quality bar: the customer master is deduplicated, and anything suspect is quarantined, not silently loaded.
  5. Cutover loses zero billed records and keeps the audit trail intact.
  6. UAT proves migrated billing behavior with real scenarios and gates go-live on signed exit criteria.

Data Model You Must Design

Your migration targets a data model you must specify, reusing the academy objects where possible:

  • Billing data: an order/invoice record set (Order/Opportunity or a custom proposal), payment status fields, payment allocation, refund records with approval status, hold/dispute records with aging and owner.
  • Documents: a naming and wiring convention for Salesforce Files/ContentDocument attached to the right Account and order — with a legacy-filename mapping table so audit questions can be answered.
  • Data quality: a suspected-duplicate and data-cleaning model — use a status or quarantine area so no suspect record reaches the live master silently; the repo's Case change-request fields and validation rules show the pattern.
  • Analytic tooling: Process_Map__c for the as-is legacy maps (M1), Business_Requirement__c with Gap_Score__c, Severity__c, Frequency__c for the fit-gap (M2/M5), UAT_Test_Case__c for the plan (M4), and User_Story__c for migration defects.

What You Will Apply

  • Phase 3: as-is process maps for the legacy flow (billing, refunds, holds, files) with rules surfaced on the map.
  • Phases 4-5: migration and cleaning requirements; the target data model and field mapping.
  • Phase 11: fit-gap matrix, severity x frequency impact scores, and configure/extend/package/build decisions.
  • Phase 12: UAT plan and test cases for migrated billing, tied to the defect flow (UAT_Defect_Logging).
  • Phase 9: automation literacy to know which gaps Flux/Approval can close before anyone says "build."

Milestones with Acceptance Criteria

M1 — As-Is Process Maps for the Legacy Flows

#Acceptance criterion
1At least three swimlanes: billing & invoicing, refunds & approvals, holds & disputes — plus one for document/file storage
2Every map has a trigger, an end, and every legacy rule or business decision annotated on the diagram
3Pain points marked, with cycle-time estimates (how long a refund takes start to finish)
4A rules inventory is separately captured: every switch, exception, or "you just know" becomes a numbered rule
5Maps recorded as Process_Map__c records with as-is metrics

M2 — Fit-Gap Matrix

#Acceptance criterion
1At least 9 legacy capabilities are compared against Salesforce (fit, partial, gap, or no fit)
2Every row is scored with severity 1-5 and frequency 1-5; impact = severity x frequency is computed and stored in Gap_Score__c
3Rows are ranked in resolve order (highest impact first), and each gap names the standard/configured capability that partially covers it
4Every "no fit" row has a decision line — configure, extend, package, or an explicit exception decision — not a default to custom build
5The matrix is traceable to requirement IDs it generated

M3 — Data Migration, Cleaning, and Quarantine Requirements

#Acceptance criterion
1Complete source-to-target field mapping for the customer master and billed records — every legacy field either maps, transforms with a rule, or is explicitly de-scoped
2Data-quality checks defined (required fields, formats, date ranges, uniqueness keys) with a pass/fail per check
3A quarantine process is defined: how a suspect record is flagged, who reviews it, and how it is restored or rejected
4Dedupe plan for the customer master (match keys, merge rules, surviving-record policy)
5Cutover plan with freeze, extract, clean, validate, load, and reconcile steps — each with entry/exit criteria

M4 — UAT Plan for Migrated Billing Scenarios

#Acceptance criterion
1UAT plan states scope, participants by role, environment, schedule, and data needs
2Scenarios cover the migrated flows: bill a freight order, apply payment, partial refund, hold, dispute resolution, statement, document retrieval
3At least 8 test cases written as steps plus expected results, each linked to a requirement and a story
4Exit criteria are numeric (e.g., 100% critical/high passed with sign-off) and agreed before testing starts
5Defect handling is wired: failures logged, assessed (severity vs priority), retested with the same steps, and the plan uses UAT_Test_Case__c + UAT_Defect_Logging

M5 — Decisions Log with Configure/Extend/Package Choices

#Acceptance criterion
1Every fit-gap row and every "no fit" capability has a decision ID, owner, and date
2Each decision records the options considered with trade-offs and the reason for the choice
3Decisions follow the escalate-in-cost-order rule: configure, then extend, then package, then build
4The log is stored/traceable to the requirements and the fit-gap rows it resolves
5No silent de-scope: anything not migrated is listed with an owner who accepted the consequence

Success Checklist

  • Every legacy billing rule is visible — on a map, in the rules inventory, in a requirement, or in an agreed de-scope — never in someone's memory
  • Fit-gap has no neutral rows: each capability is fit, partial, gap, or no fit, with an impact score
  • No "no fit" became a custom build without an AppExchange/extension evaluation first
  • UAT exit criteria are numeric and signed; the go/no-go decision is backed by criteria, not memory
  • Data quality is provable: counts of loaded, quarantined, deduplicated, and rejected records

Use Case 3 — Post-Launch Change Management

Business Context

Ninety days after the BrightLogistics CRM went live (Use Case 1's build), adoption sits at roughly 40% of target. Greg is asking hard questions. Humans being humans, the office is regressing: some dispatchers still paste leads into email, truckers never opened the app, and managers stopped looking at dashboards after week two. You are brought in with one mandate: fix adoption, not features. No new objects, no new flows — unless the diagnosis proves a simplification removes an abandonment cause.

The working theory from your phase 13 training: low adoption is usually a people-and-messaging problem, and the first deliverable is an audit that measures each persona against a baseline before any training spend.

Business Requirements

  1. Measure adoption per persona across the four usage signals: logins, record creation/update, flow runs, and report/dashboard views.
  2. Baseline (the last 4 weeks before go-live) and target (agreed with the sponsor) exist for every persona — nothing is measured "overall."
  3. Training is persona-based and includes retraining of the people most likely to regress.
  4. Communication restarts with revamped release notes and a predictable weekly channel.
  5. The sponsor gets one KPI dashboard comparing baseline to target, with drill-downs that identify which persona is lagging.
  6. A 60-day action plan assigns every action an owner and a deliver date, with KPI review points.

Data Model You Must Design

  • Usage measurement: derive login activity (login history reports), record-creation counts, flow-run evidence (the six flows' execution), and report views — describe the reports and their filters, and any adoption fields on Account/User (the academy's ChangeManagementService shows the adoption-field pattern: stage, signoff date, day count).
  • Training: the question bank Training_Question__c for assessment, plus Task/Event scheduling for sessions; personas as tracked groups so completion is measurable.
  • Feedback: the repo's change-request Case fields as the channel for "this screen fights me" reports, with routing via the case assignment rule.
  • Sponsor visibility: one dashboard backed by the two reports, each component with a drill-down.

What You Will Apply

  • Phase 13: adoption audit, training matrix, release notes revamp, comms channels, WIIFM framing.
  • Phase 10: KPI definitions, report requirements, dashboard design with drill-downs and refresh cadence.
  • Phase 6: backlog refinement — the audit findings become re-prioritized backlog items (only after diagnosis).
  • Phase 9: reading flow-run data and the automation menu to simplify away abandonment points.

Milestones with Acceptance Criteria

M1 — Adoption Audit

#Acceptance criterion
1At least 3 personas audited (dispatchers, drivers/truckers, managers — add admins)
2Each persona has a baseline %, a target %, and a deadline for the target
3Four metric types are measured or explained: logins, record activity, flow runs, report views
4The data source and collection method is named for each metric (not "feels like 40%")
5Findings are ranked by root cause (per persona) showing whether the problem is access, training, UX, or value

M2 — Persona-Based Training Plan

#Acceptance criterion
1Every persona maps to: what changes for them (WIIFM), format, duration, timing, and success measure
2Retraining of the regression-prone persona is included, not just new-hire onboarding
3Session scheduling is evidence-based (recorded as Task/Event, approved by managers)
4Each cohort has a measurable completion/competence signal (e.g., quiz via Training_Question__c)
5Trainers and materials are named; there is a plan for who covers the phone line during sessions

M3 — Release Notes Revamp and Weekly Comms Channel

#Acceptance criterion
1New release-notes template with New / Changed / Fixed sections in business language
2At least one before/after example so users know what to do differently on Monday
3A named weekly channel (meeting, email, team channel) with an owner and cadence
4A sample of the first weekly comms is drafted
5The channel answers "what does this mean for ME?" per persona

M4 — KPI Dashboard for the Sponsor

#Acceptance criterion
1Dashboard audience is Greg/sponsor; 3-5 components max on one screen
2Every component has a KPI formula, baseline vs target, chart type, and drill-down report
3At least one component identifies which persona is lagging behind the rest
4Refresh cadence and ownership are defined; the dashboard is backed by existing reports
5Each component answers "what will the viewer do when it is red?" — or it is replaced

M5 — 60-Day Action Plan with Owners

#Acceptance criterion
1Plan is phased D1-10 / D11-30 / D31-60 with a purpose per phase
2Every action has an owner and a deliver date, no orphan rows
3KPI review points are scheduled at least weekly for the adoption trend
4The plan includes gates: what proves the plan is working (per-persona trend toward target)
5The plan ends with a decision point: continue, adjust, or escalate to scope change

Success Checklist

  • An audit, not a guess, begins the engagement — before any training budget is spent
  • Adoption is measured per persona against agreed baselines and targets
  • The training plan includes retraining and has measurable cohorts
  • Comms restarted and release notes are readable by a dispatcher, not a metadata specialist
  • The sponsor dashboard lists decisions, not decorations
  • The 60-day plan is owned line-by-line and reviewed on a cadence

Final Capstone Checklist

Before you open guide 17, hold yourself to this gate. You should be able to answer "what did you decide?" for every milestone.

Portfolio completeness

  • All 15 milestones across the 3 UCs have a deliverable (no "I'll do it later")
  • Each deliverable is complete enough for a build team to implement without you
  • Every requirement is testable and traceable to a stakeholder source and a KPI
  • Every fit-gap row and de-scope has a decision owner and a documented trade-off

Repo evidence

  • At least one journey is represented end-to-end in Salesforce: objects + fields + flow/approval + a report or dashboard
  • You have deployed force-app/main/default/ to your scratch/test org and it validates
  • Test classes exist/run showing the model behaves
  • Business_Analyst permission set and Certification_Setting__mdt are part of your understanding of the environment

KPI anchoring

  • UC1: a requirement and a report prove lead-to-dispatch <4h and 80%+ auto-assignment
  • UC2: a UAT exit criterion and reconciliation step prove zero silent data loss
  • UC3: a baseline-to-target adoption KPI per persona exists

Learning check

  • You attempted the milestone before checking any answer
  • You can explain, per use case, why the delivered artifact is the right artifact

That is the brief. The work is yours. When every item above is checked, open

Phase 17: Use Case Solutions

and compare your register, your maps, your requirement list, your fit-gap, and your adoption plan against the reference artifacts — then redo the gaps. Portfolio strength comes from the redo, not the first draft.
